newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Blair faces battle with traditionalists.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Blair faces battle with traditionalists.

text.p: Tony Blair, poised to lead the British Labour Party out of the political wilderness after 17 years in opposition, could face a tough battle against traditionalists at the last party conference before a general election.

The centrist leader, a moderniser who has battled to attract the middle classes to Labour, said at the start of what could be a crucial week on the road to power: "We have undergone a huge process of change and it has been a hard, bumpy ride."

Labour now holds 20-point opinion poll lead over Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservative Party and Blair told The Observer newspaper: "If we were not New Labour, forget it. We would not be in business as a political party."

But, as delegates gathered for the party conference in the northern English seaside resort of Blackpool, two of his closest cohorts said the party's working-class roots should not be spurned in the rush to reform.
Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, warned Blair not to neglect the poor while wooing the middle class voters needed to return the party to power for the first time since 1979.
"It's very important as we reach out to these new voters, we also remember that the coalition on which we're building a Labour victory includes the dispossessed," Cook told The Sunday Times.

Deputy Labour leader John Prescott also fired a warning shot across Blair's reformist bows. "Sometimes you can go too fast. It will hit the bloody wall, the buffers. The more you pile on the change, the more and more people feel a little uneasy," he said.
Major must call a general election within the next eight months and, with the Conservatives split by divisions over Europe, unity at the Labour conference could prove a vital vote winner.
But Labour left-wingers are spoiling for a fight over such issues as pension rights, child benefit payments and worker rights.

Pensions threatened to be an emotive battleground with Lady Barbara Castle, a former Labour cabinet minister, demanding that a Labour government must restore a link between pensions and average earnings.
Party officials were trying to find a compromise to avert a conference showdown between modernisers and traditionalists.
Finance spokesman Gordon Brown, eager to avoid open-ended spending commitments, agreed to the setting up of a standing commission to review pensions policy.

If he wins the next election, Blair's toughest choice may be to decide if Britain should join the single European currency due to be launched in January 1999. The issue has sparked party mutinies among the badly-divided Conservatives.
Blair told The Observer: "My judgement is that it would be very unwise to say it is not going to happen when virtually the entire German political class is saying that it will."
Reiterating Labour's position, he said "in principle a single currency has benefits" but he insisted that economic convergence was essential if the currency was to realise them.
